newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND SEEN IN CORE EUROPE, BUT PAST DRAGS BONDS.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND SEEN IN CORE EUROPE, BUT PAST DRAGS BONDS.

text.p: History still keeps a premium on Finnish bond yields, although a strong economic trend and budget discipline have given Finland a place near the core of Europe expected to launch EMU in 1999, analysts said on Tuesday.

Especially at times when there are fears that the planned third stage of economic and monetary union would be delayed or the criteria loosened, investors require Finnish bonds to yield above the rest of the main EMU candidates' papers, they said.
"(Finland) does not have the same (core) status because of its history, but fundamentally, it takes a position in the core," said analyst Henrik Sorensen at Unibank in Copenhagen.

Finland's strong economic growth and fiscal austerity measures last year put it alongside Luxembourg to form the star duo of EU members to meet all criteria to qualify for EMU, and Finland is widely expected to meet them again this year.
But its long history of inflation and devaluations, and a ballooning public sector before the 1990s still keeps investors on their toes, the analysts said.

Postipankki chief economist Tarja Heinonen said Finland and Ireland are in a similar situation, with strong economies on one hand but on the other, more powerful neigbours -- Sweden and the UK respectively -- who do not plan to join EMU from the start, and still not enjoying full confidence among investors.
"Finland and Ireland are somewhere in between (the core and the outskirts)," she said.

Economists' forecasts for Finnish economic growth this year range between four and five percent and the finance ministry forecasts the public sector deficit at 1.4 percent and the gross public debt-to-GDP ratio at 59.3 percent.
The Maastricht criteria requires a deficit of no more than three percent of GDP and public sector debt should be or approach 60 percent of GDP.
Finnish inflation is among the lowest in the EU.

But Sorensen said investors fear that if the convergence criteria were to be loosened, Finland may use this as a leeway to boost employment -- Europe's second worst with joblessness at 16.6 percent in April -- at the expense of budget consolidation.
"I do not think so, but many in the markets do," he added.

In the week after the French socialists won the first round in the French elections on May 25, the Finnish long end yield gap over Germany rose to peak at 39 basis points, having traded around 27 basis points the week before.
The spread has since then stabilised between 30-37 basis points. The Finnish benchmark is a nine-year paper while the German maturity is 10 years.

"If there are concerns about whether (EMU) will happen, that is bad news for Finland because it reduces the likelihood that Finnish politicians will ensure Finnish competitiveness," said Wike Groenenberg, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

She said the Finnish yield gap over Germany should evaporate completely in EMU -- regardless of whether the euro will be a strong or soft currency -- since the risk of default will not differ between Finland and Germany and liquidity premiums would be very small.

But at the moment there are woes, with the German budget deficit at risky levels in relation to the Maastricht criteria, and France calling for time to study the stability pact -- an integral part of the EMU plan -- which was supposed to be ratified at an EU summit in Amsterdam next week, analysts said.
